title: Arithmetic
lines: Arithmetic is the largest block of USAT Quantitative Reasoning: about 6 of the 25 questions. Expect number facts (factors, primes, HCF and LCM, remainders), fractions and decimals, percentages, ratio and proportion, averages, profit and loss, and simple interest. There is no calculator, so the test rewards candidates who can see a short route through the numbers rather than grinding through long multiplication.
## Number facts
- A prime has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. 1 is not prime; 2 is the only even prime.
- HCF is the largest number dividing all the given numbers; LCM is the smallest number all of them divide. For two numbers, HCF × LCM = product of the numbers.
- Events that repeat every 8, 12 and 18 minutes happen together again after the LCM of the intervals, here 72 minutes.
- Divisibility: 3 or 9 when the digit sum is; 4 when the last two digits are; 8 when the last three are; 11 when the alternating digit sum (first − second + third − …) is 0 or a multiple of 11.
## Fractions, decimals and percentages
Learn the common equivalents by heart, because they turn percentage questions into fraction questions that you can do in your head.
| Fraction | Decimal | Percent
- x % of y = y % of x. So 16 % of 25 is the same as 25 % of 16, which is 4.
- A rise of r % multiplies by (1 + r/100); a fall of r % multiplies by (1 − r/100). Two successive changes multiply: +20 % then −20 % gives 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a net fall of 4 %.
- 'A is 25 % more than B' does not mean 'B is 25 % less than A'. If A = 125 and B = 100, B is 25/125 = 20 % less than A.
## Ratio and proportion
- A ratio a : b splits a total into a + b equal parts. Rs 1,200 in the ratio 3 : 5 gives 1,200 ÷ 8 = 150 per part, so Rs 450 and Rs 750.
- Direct proportion: double one, double the other (cost and quantity). Inverse proportion: double one, halve the other (workers and days at a fixed job).
## Averages
- Average = total ÷ number of items, so total = average × number. Most average questions are really total questions.
- When one item is added or removed, compare totals before and after.
## Profit, loss and simple interest
- Profit % and loss % are always on the cost price unless the question says otherwise.
- Selling price = cost × (1 + profit %/100). A 15 % discount means the buyer pays 85 % of the marked price.
- Simple interest = P × R × T ÷ 100, with T in years. Six months is T = ½.
## Worked examples
> A school has 480 students and 37.5 % of them travel by van. How many is that?
> 37.5 % = 3/8. One-eighth of 480 is 60, so 3/8 is 180 students.
> No long multiplication: change the percentage to a friendly fraction first.
> The average of 8 numbers is 25. When one number is removed, the average of the rest is 23. Which number was removed?
> Total before = 8 × 25 = 200. Total after = 7 × 23 = 161. The removed number is 200 − 161 = 39.
> A shirt marked Rs 1,600 is sold at 25 % off. The shopkeeper still makes a profit of 20 %. What did the shirt cost him?
> Selling price = 75 % of 1,600 = Rs 1,200. This is 120 % of the cost, so cost = 1,200 ÷ 1.2 = Rs 1,000.
## Mental-maths habits
- Break awkward numbers: 18 % = 10 % + 5 % + 3 %, or 20 % − 2 %.
- Cancel before multiplying: (36 × 25) ÷ 45 = (4 × 25) ÷ 5 = 20.
- Check the size of your answer against the options; one option is often wrong by a power of ten.
! Percentage change is always measured on the original value. A price that falls from Rs 500 to Rs 400 has dropped by 100/500 = 20 %, not 100/400 = 25 %.
! Profit percentage uses cost price. Dividing the profit by the selling price gives a smaller, wrong percentage that often appears as an option.
! In 'remove one item' average questions, never average the two averages; work with totals.
## Quick check
- Can you say 1/8, 3/8, 5/8 and 7/8 as percentages without thinking?
- Do you know that +x % followed by −x % always leaves a net loss?
- Can you find an LCM by listing multiples of the largest number?
- Do you turn every average question into a total question?
